tracks.name: Git & GitHub Fundamentals
tracks.description: Version control from scratch: init, stage, commit, branch, merge, and collaborate on GitHub.

lessons.title: 1. What is Version Control?
lessons.summary: Why Git exists and how it tracks changes over time.

activities.title: Imagine editing a document
activities.instruction: Without version control, you might save files as report_v1.docx, report_v2_final.docx, report_v2_final_REALLY.docx. Git solves this by tracking every change you make in a project, storing snapshots, and letting you go back to any point in time.
activities.example:
report.docx          <- the file you edit
report.docx          <- Git tracks what changed, when, and by whom

If you break something, you can undo it:
  git restore report.docx

activities.title: What does Git track?
activities.question: If you have a folder with 10 files and run `git init`, what happens?
choices: Git immediately backs up all 10 files to the cloud
Git creates a hidden .git folder that will start tracking changes going forward
Git asks you to upload each file one by one
activities.answer: Git creates a hidden .git folder that will start tracking changes going forward
activities.explanation: `git init` only creates the .git directory -- the actual tracking happens when you stage and commit files.

teaching.text: **Version control** is a system that records changes to files over time so you can recall specific versions later.
**Git** is the most popular version control system. It was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel source code.
Key concepts:

- **Repository (repo):** A project folder that Git is tracking
- **Commit:** A snapshot of your files at a specific moment
- **Branch:** An independent line of development
- **Remote:** A copy of the repo hosted on a server (like GitHub)
Git stores snapshots, not diffs. Each commit records the state of every tracked file at that point in time.

lessons.task: This is a concept lesson -- no coding needed. Click 'Continue' to move to the next lesson where you'll start using Git commands.

lessons.title: 2. Creating a Repository
lessons.summary: Turn any folder into a Git repository.

activities.title: Initialize a repository
activities.instruction: `git init` creates a hidden `.git` directory in the current folder. This directory contains all the metadata Git needs to track changes -- you never edit it directly.
activities.example:
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in ~/my-project/.git/

activities.title: What happens after init?
activities.question: After running `git init`, what does `git status` show?
choices: Nothing -- the repo is empty and has no files
An error saying no commits exist
A message that the repo is on branch main with no commits
activities.answer: A message that the repo is on branch main with no commits
activities.explanation: Git creates a default branch (usually `main`) and reports that there are no commits yet.

activities.title: Initialize your first repo
activities.instruction: Type the command to create a new Git repository in the sandbox terminal below.
activities.successCriteria: The terminal shows 'Initialized empty Git repository'

teaching.text: Every Git project starts with `git init`. This command creates the `.git` directory that stores all your version history.
git init
After running this, your folder is a Git repository. But Git doesn't track anything yet -- you need to explicitly add files.
You only run `git init` once per project. After that, Git is always watching for changes.

lessons.task: In the sandbox terminal, initialize a new Git repository by running `git init`.
hints: Type `git init` in the terminal and press Enter.
You should see 'Initialized empty Git repository in ~/my-project/.git/'

lessons.title: 3. Checking Status
lessons.summary: See what Git knows about your files.

activities.title: Reading git status
activities.instruction: `git status` tells you which branch you're on, what files are staged, what's modified but not staged, and what's untracked.
activities.example:
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	hello.txt

nothing added to commit but untracked files present

activities.title: What does 'untracked' mean?
activities.question: If a file shows as 'Untracked' in `git status`, what does that mean?
choices: Git sees the file but hasn't been told to track it yet
activities.answer: Git sees the file but hasn't been told to track it yet
activities.explanation: Untracked files exist in your folder but Git doesn't save any version of them yet. Use `git add` to start tracking.

activities.title: Check repository status
activities.instruction: First run `git init` to set up the repo, then check its status with `git status`.
activities.successCriteria: The terminal shows a status message with 'On branch main'

teaching.text: `git status` is the command you'll use most often. It tells you the current state of your repository.
git status
The output has three sections:

- **On branch main** -- which branch you're working on
- **Changes to be committed** -- files in the staging area
- **Untracked files** -- files Git sees but isn't tracking
Run `git status` often. It's the best way to understand what Git is doing.

lessons.task: In the sandbox terminal, initialize a repository and then check its status.
hints: First run `git init`, then run `git status`.
The status should show 'On branch main' and 'No commits yet'.

lessons.title: 4. Staging Changes
lessons.summary: Choose exactly what goes into your next commit.

activities.title: The staging area
activities.instruction: The staging area (or index) is a middle ground between your working directory and the repository. You `git add` files to stage them, then `git commit` to save a snapshot of what's staged.
activities.example:
$ touch hello.txt
$ git add hello.txt
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   hello.txt

activities.title: Stage a single file
activities.question: You have 3 files: a.txt, b.txt, c.txt. What command stages only a.txt?
activities.explanation: `git add .` stages everything. `git add a.txt` stages just that one file.

activities.title: Create and stage a file
activities.instruction: Create a file called hello.txt (using `touch hello.txt`), then stage it with `git add hello.txt`. Verify with `git status`.
activities.successCriteria: git status shows hello.txt under 'Changes to be committed'

teaching.text: Think of `git add` as putting files into a shopping cart before checkout. You choose what goes in; only those items get committed.

git add hello.txt      # stage one file
git add .              # stage everything
git add *.txt          # stage all .txt files
After staging, `git status` shows the file under 'Changes to be committed'.
You can unstage a file with `git restore --staged <file>`.

lessons.task: Create a file called `hello.txt` (using `touch hello.txt`), then stage it and verify with `git status`.
hints: First create the file: `touch hello.txt`
Then stage it: `git add hello.txt`
Check status: `git status` -- the file should appear under 'Changes to be committed'
lessons.solution:
git init
touch hello.txt
git add hello.txt
git status

lessons.title: 5. Saving Snapshots
lessons.summary: Lock in your changes with a commit.

activities.title: Your first commit
activities.instruction: `git commit` saves everything in the staging area as a new snapshot. Always include a message describing what changed using `-m`.
activities.example:
$ git commit -m "Add hello.txt"
[main abc1234] Add hello.txt
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 hello.txt

activities.title: Commit message etiquette
activities.question: Which commit message best describes adding a README file?
choices: Add README with project description and install instructions
activities.answer: Add README with project description and install instructions
activities.explanation: Good commit messages explain **what** changed and **why**. Avoid vague messages like 'fix stuff' or 'updated files'.

activities.title: Stage and commit
activities.instruction: Create a file, stage it, and make your first commit with a message.
activities.successCriteria: git log shows the commit with your message

teaching.text: A commit is a permanent snapshot of your staged files. Every commit gets a unique hash (like `abc1234`) and records who made it and when.
git commit -m "Your message here"
After committing, the staging area is cleared. Your changes are now safely stored in the repository.
Write commit messages in the imperative mood: 'Add feature' not 'Added feature'. Start with a capital letter and keep it under 72 characters.

lessons.task: Create a file called `README.md`, stage it, and commit it with the message 'Add README'.
hints: Create the file: `touch README.md`
Stage it: `git add README.md`
Commit with a message: `git commit -m "Add README"`
lessons.solution:
git init
touch README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"

lessons.title: 6. Viewing History
lessons.summary: See the timeline of commits in your project.

activities.title: Reading git log
activities.instruction: `git log` shows the commit history in reverse chronological order. Each entry shows the commit hash, author, date, and message.
activities.example:
$ git log
commit abc1234567890 (HEAD -> main)
Author: You <you@example.com>
Date:   Thu Aug 22 10:30:00 2026

    Add README

commit def0987654321
Author: You <you@example.com>
Date:   Thu Aug 22 10:00:00 2026

    Initial commit

activities.title: What does HEAD mean?
activities.question: In `git log` output, what does `(HEAD -> main)` tell you?
choices: You are currently on the main branch, and HEAD points to the latest commit
activities.answer: You are currently on the main branch, and HEAD points to the latest commit
activities.explanation: HEAD is a pointer to the current commit. `HEAD -> main` means you're on the main branch.

activities.title: Make commits and view history
activities.instruction: Make two commits, then run `git log` to see the history.
activities.successCriteria: git log shows at least two commits

teaching.text: `git log` is your project's timeline. It shows every commit from newest to oldest.

git log              # full log
git log --oneline     # compact: one line per commit
Each commit has:

- **Hash** -- a unique ID like `abc1234`
- **Author** -- who made the change
- **Date** -- when it was made
- **Message** -- what the commit does
Press `q` to exit the log viewer if it opens in a pager.

lessons.task: Make two separate commits (each with a different file and message), then run `git log` to see the history.
hints: First commit: create a file, `git add` it, then `git commit -m "First commit"`
Second commit: create another file, `git add` it, then `git commit -m "Second commit"`
Then run `git log` to see both commits
lessons.solution:
git init
touch file1.txt
git add file1.txt
git commit -m "First commit"
touch file2.txt
git add file2.txt
git commit -m "Second commit"
git log

lessons.title: 7. Seeing Changes

activities.title: Reading a diff
activities.instruction: `git diff` shows line-by-line changes in your working directory. Lines prefixed with `-` were removed; lines prefixed with `+` were added.
activities.example:
$ echo "Hello" > greet.txt
git add greet.txt
git commit -m "Add greet"
$ echo "Hello, World" > greet.txt
$ git diff
diff --git a/greet.txt b/greet.txt
--- a/greet.txt
+++ b/greet.txt
@@ -1 +1 @@
-Hello
+Hello, World

activities.title: What does diff show?
activities.question: If you modify a file but don't `git add` it, what does `git diff` show?
choices: Nothing -- you need to commit first
The difference between the working file and the last commit
activities.answer: The difference between the working file and the last commit
activities.explanation: `git diff` compares your working directory to the last commit (HEAD). Staging doesn't matter for this comparison.

activities.title: See a diff
activities.instruction: Create and commit a file, then modify it and run `git diff`.
activities.successCriteria: git diff shows the change you made

teaching.text: `git diff` shows you exactly what changed, line by line.

git diff                 # working dir vs HEAD
git diff --staged         # staged vs HEAD
git diff HEAD~1           # vs one commit back
The output uses `+` for added lines and `-` for removed lines.
Run `git diff` before committing to review your changes one last time.

lessons.task: Create a file called `note.txt` with content 'v1', commit it, then change it to 'v2' and run `git diff`.
hints: 1. `touch note.txt`, `echo v1 > note.txt`, `git add note.txt`, `git commit -m "v1"`
2. `echo v2 > note.txt`, `git diff`
lessons.solution:
git init
touch note.txt
echo v1 > note.txt
git add note.txt
git commit -m "v1"
echo v2 > note.txt
git diff

lessons.title: 8. Creating Branches
lessons.summary: Work on features in parallel without affecting main.

activities.title: Branches are pointers
activities.instruction: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. When you create a branch, Git makes a new pointer. The `*` marks which branch you're on.
activities.example:
$ git branch
* main

$ git branch feature

$ git branch
  feature
* main

activities.title: Does branching copy files?
activities.question: When you run `git branch feature`, does Git duplicate all the files?
choices: Yes -- it creates a full copy of the project
No -- it just creates a pointer to the current commit
It depends on the file size
activities.answer: No -- it just creates a pointer to the current commit
activities.explanation: Branches are lightweight. Git only creates a new pointer (a 41-byte file), not a copy of the project.

activities.title: Create and list branches
activities.instruction: Make an initial commit, then create a branch called `feature` and list all branches.

teaching.text: Branches let you work on different features simultaneously without affecting the main codebase.

git branch feature     # create a new branch
git branch             # list branches

  feature
* main                  # * = current branch
Creating a branch doesn't switch to it. Use `git checkout feature` or `git switch feature` to move to the new branch.
Branches are a core part of the Git workflow. The `main` branch is typically the stable, production-ready code.

lessons.task: Make an initial commit, create a branch called `feature`, then list all branches.
hints: 1. Create and commit a file to initialize the repo
2. Run `git branch feature`
3. Run `git branch` to see both branches
lessons.solution:
git init
touch app.js
git add app.js
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git branch feature
git branch

lessons.title: 9. Switching Branches
lessons.summary: Move between branches to work on different features.

activities.title: Switching context
activities.instruction: `git switch` (or `git checkout`) moves you to a different branch. Your working directory updates to match that branch's files.
activities.example:
$ git switch feature
Switched to branch 'feature'

$ git branch
* feature
  main

activities.title: What happens to your files?
activities.question: You're on `main` with file A.txt. You switch to `feature` which has file B.txt. What happens?
activities.explanation: Switching branches updates your working directory to match the target branch. Files unique to the old branch are removed, and files unique to the new branch appear.

activities.title: Switch between branches
activities.instruction: Create two branches with different files, then switch between them and verify the files change.
activities.successCriteria: git branch shows the current branch changed after each switch

teaching.text: `git switch` is the modern way to change branches. The older `git checkout` does the same thing but also handles other tasks.

git switch feature     # move to feature branch
git switch main        # move back to main
When you switch, Git updates your working directory to match the target branch's commit.
Use `git switch -c new-branch` to create a branch and switch to it in one step.

lessons.task: Create a branch, switch to it, then switch back. Verify with `git branch` each time.
hints: 1. Initialize and commit to create the repo
2. Create a branch: `git branch feature`
3. Switch to it: `git switch feature`
4. Switch back: `git switch main`
lessons.solution:
git init
touch app.js
git add app.js
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git branch feature
git switch feature
git switch main

lessons.title: 10. Merging Branches
lessons.summary: Combine branches to bring work together.

activities.title: Fast-forward merge
activities.instruction: When you merge a branch that is ahead of your current branch, Git does a 'fast-forward' -- it simply moves the pointer forward.
activities.example:
$ git switch main
$ git merge feature
Updating abc1234..def5678
Fast-forward
 1 file changed, 10 insertions(+)

activities.title: Which branch receives the changes?
activities.question: You're on `main` and run `git merge feature`. Where do the changes go?
activities.explanation: The branch you're on (main) receives the changes from the branch you specify (feature).

activities.title: Merge a branch
activities.instruction: Create a commit on main, create a branch and add another commit, then merge the branch back into main.
activities.successCriteria: git log shows the merge commit or fast-forward on main

teaching.text: `git merge` brings changes from one branch into another. It's how you combine parallel work.

git switch main          # make sure you're on the target branch
git merge feature        # merge feature into main
There are two types of merges:

- **Fast-forward**: The target branch is behind. Git just moves the pointer.
- **Merge commit**: Both branches diverged. Git creates a new commit combining both.
After merging, you can safely delete the feature branch with `git branch -d feature`.

lessons.task: Create a branch, add a commit to it, switch back to main, and merge the branch.
hints: 1. Initialize and commit on main
2. Create and switch to a feature branch
3. Add a commit on the feature branch
4. Switch back to main: `git switch main`
5. Merge: `git merge feature`
lessons.solution:
git init
touch app.js
git add app.js
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git branch feature
git switch feature
touch feature.js
git add feature.js
git commit -m "Add feature"
git switch main
git merge feature

lessons.title: 11. Cloning Repositories
lessons.summary: Copy an existing repository from GitHub to your machine.

activities.title: Copying a repo
activities.instruction: `git clone` downloads a complete copy of a remote repository, including all its history and branches.
activities.example:
$ git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
Cloning into 'repo'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 12, done.
remote: Total 12 (delta 2), reused 10 (delta 1)
Receiving objects: 100% (12/12), done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (2/2), done.

activities.title: What does clone give you?
activities.question: After cloning a repo, what do you have on your machine?
choices: The complete history, all branches, and all files
activities.answer: The complete history, all branches, and all files
activities.explanation: Clone gives you everything -- every commit, every branch, every file. It's a full copy.

activities.title: Clone a repository
activities.instruction: Clone the simulated remote repository `https://github.com/example/my-app.git`.
activities.successCriteria: The terminal shows 'Cloning into' and the clone completes

teaching.text: `git clone` is how you get a copy of someone else's project. It creates a new folder and downloads everything.
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
After cloning, the repo has a remote called `origin` that points to the URL you cloned from.
You typically clone once, then use `git pull` to stay up to date.

lessons.task: Clone the repository `https://github.com/example/my-app.git` using the sandbox terminal.
hints: Run: `git clone https://github.com/example/my-app.git`
You should see 'Cloning into 'my-app'...'

lessons.title: 12. Push and Pull
lessons.summary: Share your work and sync with GitHub.

activities.title: Sending and receiving changes
activities.instruction: `git push` uploads your commits to GitHub. `git pull` downloads and integrates new commits from GitHub.
activities.example:
# Push your commits to GitHub:
$ git push origin main
Enumerating objects: 5, done.
Total 3 (delta 1), reused 0 (delta 0)
To https://github.com/user/repo.git
   a1b2c3d..e4f5g6h  main -> main

# Pull new changes from GitHub:
$ git pull
remote: Enumerating objects: 4, done.
Unpacking objects: 100% (2/2), done.
From https://github.com/user/repo
   e4f5g6h..h7i8j9k  main -> origin/main
Updating e4f5g6h..h7i8j9k
Fast-forward

activities.title: Push before pull?
activities.question: If your local branch is behind the remote, what should you do first?
choices: git push to force your version
git pull to get the latest changes first
activities.answer: git pull to get the latest changes first
activities.explanation: Always pull first to get others' changes, resolve any conflicts, then push your work.

activities.title: Push and pull
activities.instruction: Clone a repo, make a commit, push it, then pull to sync.
activities.successCriteria: Both push and pull commands complete successfully

teaching.text: `git push` sends your commits to the remote (like GitHub). `git pull` downloads and merges changes from the remote.

git push origin main     # push main to GitHub
git pull                 # pull and merge changes
The workflow is: make changes locally, commit them, then push. Before starting new work, pull to get the latest.
GitHub is the most popular Git hosting service. It provides a web interface for code review, issues, and collaboration.

lessons.task: Clone a repo, create and commit a file, push it, then pull to sync.
hints: 1. `git clone https://github.com/example/repo.git`
2. `cd repo`, create a file, `git add` and `git commit`
3. `git push origin main`
4. `git pull`
lessons.solution:
git clone https://github.com/example/repo.git
cd repo
touch newfile.txt
git add newfile.txt
git commit -m "Add new file"
git push origin main
git pull
